scenarios.title: Fake Customer Payment / Account Credential Theft
scenarios.attacker_objective: Use a fake customer/payment interaction to persuade the business owner to visit a fraudulent payment page and expose business account credentials, creating an opportunity for account compromise.

questions.story:
10:18 AM — A New Customer

You are running your small online business and receive a message from a customer you have never dealt with before.

“Hi, I have just made payment for the items. Please confirm it so you can start preparing my order. I’m in a hurry, so please use the payment confirmation link I sent.”

There is a link in the message. You check your usual payment account, but you cannot see a payment yet.
questions.question: What would you do next?
options: Open the link because the customer says the payment has already been made.
Ask the customer to send their account password so you can verify them.
Check the payment independently through the business's normal bank/mobile-money/payment platform before taking any action.
Send the link to another customer and ask whether it looks legitimate.
questions.feedback: The safest choice is to verify the payment independently through the trusted payment platform. The customer's link should not become the source of truth for whether money was received.

questions.story:
10:24 AM — The Customer Becomes Persistent

You have not opened the link.

The customer says the payment is already processing and that the confirmation page needs your business email login before the payment can be released. You notice that the website address does not match the normal payment service your business uses.
questions.question: What is the strongest warning sign at this point?
options: The customer is ordering several products.
The customer is asking for a business email password through an unfamiliar payment page.
The customer says the order is urgent.
The customer sent the message through social media.
questions.feedback: The strongest indicator is the request for a business email password through an unfamiliar payment page. The payment story is being used as a path to obtain credentials.

questions.story:
10:31 AM — The Attack Develops

You did not provide the password. The customer continues insisting that you log in through the link. At almost the same time, you receive a security notification saying someone has attempted to access one of your business accounts from an unfamiliar device.

You now have an unexpected payment claim, a suspicious payment link requesting business credentials, and an unfamiliar account-access attempt.
questions.question: What is most likely happening?
options: The payment system is performing a normal update.
The customer is helping you complete the payment.
The payment interaction is likely being used as a phishing attempt, with the attacker trying to obtain access to a business account.
The customer's phone has probably lost internet connection.
questions.feedback: The sequence points to a credential-phishing and account-compromise attempt. The attacker is using a believable payment situation to create an opportunity to obtain access.
